utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Your Honours. Thank you, Your Honours, and good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Djordjevic.

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: If we could bring, immediately, P137.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: This is an order or a dispatch of the 18th of March, 1999, I think signed by you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: If we could look at the next page in B/C/S. Could we look at the bottom in B/C/S of this page.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Signed on your behalf, and it dispatches PJP personnel on rotation to Kosovo. And I think you indicated that this was the classical or the standard type of dispatch, and we have seen many of those in evidence.

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Was this a -- was this document necessary or required before PJP personnel could be sent from the SUPs in Serbia on assignment in Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it was required.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And I -- well, that's out of the question. They were required to be signed by you or at least signed in the capacity of the chief of public security?

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: After the decision of the minister, this was a logistical matter. Most frequently it would be signed by me, but given that this is a routine activity, if I happened to be absent -- it simply didn't depend on my signature or on somebody else's signature. These units had to be replaced and new units had to be sent pursuant to the decision of the minister, so this is a purely technical matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Yeah, could it be signed by anybody or in the capacity of anybody but the chief of public security?

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, we have seen that documents like these were signed by others. They were signed by me but by others as well. As I have told you, this is a purely formal matter. This is not a decision that anything else depended upon. This simply gave information on what direction the units should take, to whom they should report, what funds they were to be given. These were just the routine instructions that were normally given.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: But I see that all of them that we have - and there are quite a few of them in evidence - are signed either by you or by someone else for you as chief of public security. Is there a reason for that?

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what you have in mind when you ask "is there a reason." I don't know how to answer this.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Well, could any other functionary in the public security section issue those dispatches or orders?

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I have said, this is not an order on activating units. This is a purely formal matter, giving information on which unit was to go where. It could have been signed by anybody else; but given that it was being sent to a number of secretariats, then they used my authority or somebody who was in my position. So I happened to sign this most frequently, but there were also many cases where instead of me some other person signed it.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Could we move on to look at P144. Incidentally, before we get to this document, did the minister -- did the minister's order deploying the PJP to Kosovo, was that a written order?

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your question is not precise enough. Pursuant to a written order of deploying PJP in Kosovo -- there were actually no written orders deploying PJPs in Kosovo by minister. Minister would issue a decision saying that such and such units were to be sent to Kosovo in order to carry out tasks. Following that, there would be this technical action taken that units are to report to the staff, that they're placed at the disposal of the staff, and that the staff could use those units pursuant to the decision of the minister on establishing the staff of anti-terrorist activities in Kosovo.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Yes, but the decision of the minister, saying that such units were to be sent to Kosovo in order to carry out tasks, was that decision or those decisions written decisions?

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. As far as I know, those were verbal orders both for special police unit and for Special Anti-Terrorist Unit and for the special operations unit of the state security department.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And you cannot recall at any time these deployments being the subject of any written orders by the minister?

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The order of the minister on establishing the staff specified that all attached units were to be placed at the disposal of the staff, that the staff planned their activities and was in charge and had the command over those activities. Therefore, based on that decision, the minister basically authorised the staff to be in charge of all the units that had been attached and were sent there. He did not write orders specifying that such and such a unit was sent to Kosovo and so on. No. Those orders were verbal. However, the attachment of units to the staff in Kosovo was regulated in the decision on establishing the staff in Kosovo.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Okay. Before you -- we could move on. Before you we have a decision transferring or terminating or a decision of the completion of deployment of Mr. Milan Cankovic. Who had been carrying out tasks -- MUP staff tasks in Pristina. This one is signed by you. And we have seen others like this. Without going through them, apart from yourself or the minister, was any other functionary in the MUP authorised to sign these documents as terminating or appointing to certain positions -- well, not certain positions, to positions in the MUP staff? And since that question is a little bit muddled, let me just ask it again. You signed some of these orders, and I think we have seen where the minister signed some of these orders. Apart from you or the minister, was any other functionary in the MUP entitled or authorised to sign orders terminating or appointing MUP staff?

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Nobody else except for minister could issue decisions on sending somebody to perform duties of a member of the staff in Pristina. That type of decision could only be issued by the minister. The minister could authorise me to issue a decision on terminating somebody's engagement in Kosovo or a decision regulating some matters of employment status relating to salary and so on. But I could issue such decisions only pursuant to an authorisation of the minister.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Yes, and --

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: And I did issue such decisions.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And these decisions, only you were -- and I'm just asking based on those that I have seen and those which are in evidence here. Only you were authorised to sign these orders?

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. In cases where minister authorised me, then I in accordance with the then-existing regulations could act in accordance with the authorisation given by him. I think that some other officials did not receive that type of authorisation from the minister.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: By what means - and I'm moving on to another topic quite quickly since we are moving quickly this morning - by what means did you communicate with the special unit commanders, PJP commanders, members of the staff, people like Mr. Lukic and Mr. Stevanovic during March, April, May of 1999? I think you said earlier you had been in contact with them when the telephone lines were up and running. And you certainly wasn't -- well, you were certainly in contact with them during this period, especially when some of the personnel were killed, you would be in touch with them on that score. But by what means would you be in touch with them?

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, you have quite expanded the circle of people to whom I talked during the war in Kosovo. I have already stated here that I didn't speak to any SUP chiefs or commanders of PJP units during the war. I also didn't speak to the commander or the commanders of the special unit either, except in relation to Kosovo-related events. After that, I had absolutely no contacts with any other unit commanders or any other chief of SUP. As I have said to you, I occasionally spoke to Sreten Lukic or Obrad. I would normally speak to them if I was supposed to go down to Kosovo and I would call them up and say, "I'm coming down, where are we going to meet?" This is when I went on the 18th or –-that's actually when this was. So this is how I communicated with them.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Okay. Very well --

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If they had some sort of information on some members being killed --

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: You would call them by what means?

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the telephone when possible. I had no other means of communication. If the telephone worked, then, yes, I could talk to them concerning the matters that I have just described to you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Did you mention just now mobile telephones?

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't say that. I said simply "by telephone if possible." I didn't say "mobile telephone."

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Were there any types of special communications or any special means of communicating with them apart from the telephones? In case of emergency, for example.

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were experts here who answered in detail your questions --

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: No, no. No --

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- here and their task was to inform you in detail on means of communication. I wasn't aware of any other means of communication except telephone when possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: That's what I'm asking. I'm not asking you -- I'm asking you what you did, which is of the principal importance here.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Your Honours, if I could bring up 06004.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Is this document an exhibit that's presently on the screen?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, it's already exhibited.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: That's P137, is that it?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: No, I think it's P144 now on the screen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: This is the record of the testimony of Mr. Slobodan Borisavljevic before the district court in Belgrade on the 2nd of March, 2004. And just to orient yourself, Slobodan Borisavljevic in 1999 was your chef de cabinet; that's correct?

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that he was during some period of time in 1999 as well. Whether there was a change in the meantime, I can't remember, but yes he was.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Could we look at page 8 of the English. And I think that's also page 8 of the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Are you, Mr. Djordjevic, seeing a point where the deputy Prosecutor asks: "Were you getting the reports on movements of your units and their activities in Kosovo?"

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't see it here. I see that he says that there had been some reports where there was no information on the crimes. I see that in the beginning, but I don't see what you are referring me to.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I think I probably have it wrong -- is it there -- I understand it is there now. He said: "General information went through dispatches about the important events, but specifically about this activities considering the war circumstances everything was hindered and I think we weren't getting it. Mainly that went orally, through the special communications that we had." And the deputy Prosecutor asked: "Who received these oral reports?" And Mr. Borisavljevic said: "General Djordjevic received oral reports, according to the lines of work, chiefs of administrations, and from the Chief of Staff. The Chief of Staff was at that time now Colonel -- at that time General, now Colonel, Sreten Lukic, who contacted directly by telephone by the special" -- and I don't think the translator got it, "but contacted by telephone by the special General Djordjevic." And he was asked: "... what did these reports refer to?" And he said: "Well, they referred to -- concretely in the case of Kosovo and Metohija, they referred to the terrorist activity of these Albanian terrorists. It means at the time I know that in the period from December all until the beginning of the bombardment there were especially wide and intensive activities of the Albanian terrorists." Firstly, what special communications is he referring to, do you know?

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Throughout Serbia, there was a system of special communications which was discussed here by experts from that field. However, during the war - as they also said - due to damage of the relay systems, these special systems would either work or would not work. So that is one question, and you were informed about that in detail here. What Slobodan Borisavljevic is speaking of here are questions that are contained in regular reports that we had occasion to see quite a few times here. So this has to do with regular information about significant events and occurrences in Kosovo. One particular piece of information had to do with the activity of Albanian terrorists. So there is not a single report here or a single piece of information that had come here, as he says here, that I spoke on the telephone. He was in another office and then he knows that I spoke on the phone -- but never mind. In all his reports that we saw here, he made no claims that I was ever informed about how and in which way units were being used in anti-terrorist or combat activities. So he is speaking arbitrarily here about me speaking to them. And secondly, in everything we saw him say here, there is no reference to combat reports from Kosovo because there weren't any.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Well, he says quite specifically upon the specific question being asked that you received oral reports from General Lukic about the anti-terrorist activities in Kosovo. Wouldn't your chef de cabinet -- wouldn't your chef de cabinet be in a position to know what reports you are receiving?

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Oh, please, please. Could you be more precise. Please. He did not say that I was communicator over the telephone with Sreten Lukic about anti-terrorist activity, that is to say combat activity of the units that were down there.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What he's talking about here is --

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Let me read what he says.

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, do read it.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Maybe there is a translation issue. He says: "General Djordjevic received oral reports according to the lines of work, chiefs of the administrations, and from the Chief of Staff, Chief of Staff was at the time General, now Colonel Sreten Lukic, who contacted directly by telephone by the special General Djordjevic. "... what did these reports refer to?" And later on: "Well, they referred to concretely in the case of Kosovo and Metohija, they referred to the terrorist activities of these Albanian terrorists ..." That's what he's saying. Sreten Lukic reported to you about the --

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Oh, please. He is saying here in principle that he received oral reports, General Djordjevic received oral reports, concerning lines of work from chiefs of administrations.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And what does he say about Sreten Lukic, what does he say about that?

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't even know what Slobodan Borisavljevic is saying, let alone Sreten Lukic. So Slobodan Borisavljevic does not say here whether I spoke twice or three times during the time war was being waged there, let alone could he say what it was that I discussed with Sreten Lukic. So this is a very general matter. Of course he, as the chef de cabinet, knew that over the telephone I could talk. Now, whether I did talk, how many times, what it was that we discussed, that is something that the chef de cabinet does not know. He is making assumptions here.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: And whether I spoke five times during this period of time or twice, how could he know? He is not saying that I had regular contacts and that he reported to me about this and that and that I ordered him to do this or that. He was no witness of that kind. He does not know about that. I had my own office. The telephone was in my own office. I had my own telephone. He doesn't know about this. He was not present when I made telephone -- my own telephone conversations. His assumptions can be whatever.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: So I think that's the answer to my question. The question was: You are saying that your chef de cabinet does not know or would not know who was reporting up to you and what the reports were? Is that what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The chef de cabinet was not with me in my office when I talked to any chief of administration, either in person or over the telephone. He was not in my office when I spoke to Sreten Lukic or Obrad Stevanovic or to the minister or any other person; he cannot testify about that. He cannot know whether I had contacts, how many contacts, let alone about what it was that we had discussed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: During the war, March, April, May, June, you -- did you become aware of protests and complaints by leading figures in the international community about allegations of crimes committed against civilians by the security forces in Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And while we are waiting for that answer, could we bring up 65 ter number 00399.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Did you hear of the complaints or the protests from persons in the international arena about allegations of the misconduct of the Serb -- of the forces of the FRY and Serbia, the police and the army, in Kosovo in respect to their treatment of civilians?

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I can see --

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- this was sent on the 26th of March, 1999, to President Milan Milutinovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Mr. Djordjevic, I will ask you about this shortly and you will be able to say what you want. I'm just asking you during that period, March, April, May, June 1999, did you hear that there were allegations that the forces of the FRY and Serbia, that is the VJ and the MUP, in Kosovo were committing crimes against civilians, Kosovo Albanian civilians?

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No letter was sent to me from these international structures. I was not aware of any crimes. I've already told you what it was that I knew about or these claims from international institutions. My attention, my attention was primarily focused on the territory of Serbia outside Kosovo and Metohija. That is what I was responsible for to the minister, and really at that time I was not in a position to read this or did anyone send me personally any letter from international representatives.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Yes. I wanted to make a distinction here so you understand what I'm asking you. I'm not asking whether or not the crimes were committed or whether you knew that crimes were committed; I'm asking you about allegations that there were crimes committed against Kosovo Albanian civilians in Kosovo. Are you saying that in that period you never even heard a whisper of an allegation that crimes were being committed against Kosovo Albanian civilians by the Serbian security forces?

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I had no concrete knowledge, nor did I read about or did I hear about any reports or letters that were sent to one address or several addresses from these structures. As for general stories, general knowledge, perhaps there was something like that to the effect that something was happening somewhere. There was a war going on. I did not know anything specific or did I have the task to do anything in relation to that. So I was not familiarised with these documents that were sent by the international community. They were not sent to me. And I had no opportunity to familiarise myself with what they were saying. In the territory that I was responsible for, at that period of time there was terrible destruction going on and terrible crimes were being committed. So my --

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- attention was focused on what --

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Yes, I -- we know about the rest of Serbia and that there was a war going on. Well, let us look at this letter. This was sent to the head of the Serbian government, Mr. Milutinovic, somebody that you would attend meetings in his presence. It refers to the current reports of escalating violence in Kosovo, and I'm looking at the second paragraph.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And maybe, just for the record, I should say that this is a letter of the 26th of March, 1999, from Louise Arbour, then-Prosecutor of this Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And it says: "... in the light of current reports of escalating violence in Kosovo, I am gravely concerned that serious violations of international humanitarian law continue to be committed." And she also in the last paragraph says: "Meanwhile, I believe that everything must be done to deter the commission of future crimes. I therefore look to you to exercise your authority over your subordinates; to exercise your leadership in order to prevent the commission of further crimes ..." The question, Mr. Djordjevic, is not whether or not you got this letter, but were you not aware that the Prosecutor of this Tribunal had sent a letter expressing grave concern about the allegations - and I repeat the word allegations - of crimes being committed in Kosovo against Kosovo Albanian civilians?

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, what I heard in the interpretation was that Milan Milutinovic was the prime minister of Serbia. He was not the prime minister. He was the president of Serbia. As for Milan Milutinovic, I attended a meeting with him on the 4th of May, 1999, the first time, and this has to do with the 26th of March. Now, who wrote to him and what was written to him -- at this meeting where I was present and where Milutinovic was present, he did not mention this letter at all. Now, how am I to know what representatives of the international community wrote about to him? How would I know that? And he is not duty-bound to report to me about what was being written to him, so ...

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Well, I -- you know, you leave me in a position to infer what your answer is. Can you not answer the question directly? Did you become aware that the Prosecutor of this Tribunal had sent a letter expressing grave concern about the allegations of crimes against Kosovo Albanian civilians?

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What you presented to me is this letter. I've already told you that I saw Milan Milutinovic when I saw him, and that was almost two months after he received this letter. So I did not know what the representatives of the international community were writing about to Milan Milutinovic or to others, nor were they duty-bound to report to me about what it was that they had received in terms of any indications of certain things that they were writing about.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Did you --

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: So I was not aware of what was written here.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Did you at any time hear from any source that there were allegations that unlawful violence was being committed against Kosovo Albanian civilians by Serbian security forces?

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've been telling you several times now what my duty was and what my obligations were. Please understand, every night, every day, Serbia was bombed. Serbia -- apart from Kosovo, and Kosovo was as well. My duty, my obligation, was to follow this. That is what I was aware of. That was my province of work given to me by the minister.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Mr. Djordjevic, you refuse to directly answer my questions. I'll break it down -- I'll break it down --

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What do you mean refuse? I have been telling you. I was not aware of crimes being committed. I did not know that the representatives of the international community wrote to Milutinovic or anyone else about crimes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Mr. Djordjevic, I again make the distinction, and I want you to focus on the question. I'm not saying crimes were committed, I'm not asking you if you are aware that crimes were committed. I'm asking you if you were aware that there were allegations, if you ever heard during that period, March, April, May, June, allegations or that there were allegations that there were these crimes being committed?

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I had not heard of these allegations.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Very well. In July, August, September, October, November, December, the remainder of 1999, did you hear from any source that there were allegations that there were crimes committed against Kosovo Albanian civilians by Serbian security forces?

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Afterwards, when all of this was over, there were some complaints, but I really did not know anything specific. There was a war going on, and every war is accompanied by crime. There is not a single war that does not involve crimes as well, and that falls within the general context of the situation that existed. I was aware that perhaps there may have been a crime committed somewhere, like in any other war, but I was not there to... I don't know what, process all crimes and respond to everything. There is not a single war without war crimes. So in that very general understanding of war and consequences --

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Djordjevic, I'm not asking you such a general question, you know, that there are crimes in war, et cetera. I'm asking you about your state of mind, and I keep having to repeat these questions. I'm asking you about a more narrow thing. Did it come to your attention after the war, in the six months -- the remaining six months of 1999 after the war, that there were allegations that the forces of the FRY and Serbia, that the VJ and the MUP forces committed crimes against Kosovo Albanian civilians during the war?

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: How could I know about that? Should I base knowledge on the knowledge of representatives of the international community?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Just for the record, you know, you haven't answered my question, but I'm just going to ask for the record: In 2000 -- in the year 2000, you remained as chief of the public security department for all of 2000, even after Mr. Stojiljkovic had been sacked. Did you in the year 2000 become aware that there were allegations that Serbian security forces, that is, the VJ and the MUP, were involved in crimes against Kosovo Albanian civilians?

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've been telling you several times now, I did not know of any specific event that I learned of immediately after the war or later that would indicate a concrete crime and concrete perpetrators. What I have was something in very general terms, that something may have happened somewhere, like anywhere else. So I did not have any knowledge about any one of these crimes that are being charged here or these localities where this had happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Your Honours, the letter 00399, I tender that and ask that it be received in evidence as exhibit -- and be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that will be Exhibit P1511.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It's pointed out to me, Mr. Stamp, we saw but you have not sought to tender a transcript of proceedings before the Belgrade district court. Did you mean to tender that or not?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, I -- having asked the witness questions about it, I think it could come before the Court for its consideration.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: That -- Mr. Djurdjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Two things: First of all, that transcript was not tendered, and I don't think it can be tendered. It has to do with a statement given before a different court, and it was not confirmed by the witness. It has to do with a person who was put on the Prosecutor's witness list, and the Prosecutor gave up on that person. I believe that there are no grounds for having that document admitted into evidence. What Mr. Stamp presented, we said that that would be all right, on the basis of your decision that the witness can say what the situation was, but I don't think that this transcript can be admitted with regard to a person who had not testified before this Court. I believe that that would suffice. I wanted something else to say in relation to something completely different now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: We're right with you and ahead of you on the transcript. No need to say any more about that. It will merely be marked for identification. It will not become an exhibit.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that will be Exhibit P1512, marked for identification.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Now, you had something else?

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, yes. I don't understand what Mr. Djordjevic has to do with this document. He saw it now. He said that he had never received it and never seen it. Now just because Mr. Stamp presented it to him now it is being admitted into evidence in this way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I suspect, Mr. Djurdjic, we would be in the hundreds of documents tendered by you and the Prosecution in this case to which that comment might have been made. It is a document of direct relevance to the case. We know the witness says he knew nothing of it, and we will see by the end of the case whether there is anything that changes that position or not. So it's received as an exhibit.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And while we are at it, could we -- may I ask, has it been given a number? Thank you. Could we have a look at 00398.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: This is another letter from the Prosecutor of the Tribunal in the same terms, to the President of the Federal Republic, Mr. Milosevic. Were you aware at any time that the Prosecutor of these Tribunals -- of this Tribunal had sent a letter expressing these grave concerns and also requesting that steps be taken to deter the commission of future crimes?

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Just like I said in relation to the previous letter, I was totally unaware of this letter too.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: But did you hear about it in any way at any time?

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, not about this letter.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Your Honours, I also tender this document and ask that it be received in evidence. I understand that it would be -- it's a matter for the Court to give it whatever weight it merits as the case develops.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: At the moment, it may do nothing more than fill in a minor element of historical continuity.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: But for the reasons indicated, it too will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that will be Exhibit P1513.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Could we look at P42.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: This is a -- an indictment issued in May 1999, on the 22nd of May, 1999, and it became public, I think, on the -- well, it became public on the 27th of May, 1999. Among the indictees are the president, Milosevic, that's the federal president; the Serbian president, Milutinovic; and Mr. Sainovic; Mr. Ojdanic, the head of the VJ; and also Mr. Stojiljkovic. And I remind you of your evidence, Mr. Djordjevic, your office was always neighbouring Mr. Stojiljkovic's office during the war. You were always in the same place. Did you -- or when did you become aware of this indictment?

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, at this particular moment, I cannot give you any specific date. Probably on the date when it became public, just like every other citizen, I also learned about this indictment.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Well, your minister, the man with whom you shared an office and whose instructions you obeyed according to your testimony, is indicted here. Did you also discover at the time when you learned about it what he was being indicted for?

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, no. I only learned that it was relating to Kosovo, that the indictment was issued for Kosovo. However, as for the content of the indictment, I really at that point in time wasn't much interested in that nor did anybody tell me to what the indictment pertained. I had no information about the charges that were raised against all these people named here.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Well, did you obtain or try to obtain a copy of the indictment and have a look at it?

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: It is interesting that you say that you were not interested in that because you have said that on the orders of the minister you participated in the concealment of bodies that you knew came from Kosovo. Now, you see that the minister is indicted and you are not interested to find out what he's indicted for? Is that what you're telling the Court?

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm telling you that I never had an opportunity to see a copy of the indictments, to read the allegations contained therein. I don't know how it was possible for me to find out what the allegations were. So believe me that I never studied this indictment. I only knew this general indication that it related to Kosovo, but I didn't know any details.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: The -- did you know if Mr. Stojiljkovic, who was in a neighbouring office, had a copy of this?

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really didn't know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Did you ask him?

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: So I didn't know. According to the indictment and generally speaking with regard to this institution, he had his own attitude and views. He wasn't interested either. As far as I knew what the indictment contained, I think that he wasn't particularly interested in that. So I know what his attitude towards the indictment was. I don't know if he received a copy, whether he studied it. I know nothing about that, apart from his general attitude towards this institution and the charges raised against him.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Did you inquire of him whether he had a copy of this indictment and did you discuss the indictment with him at all?

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I never discussed that with him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Djurdjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, it seems to me that after the witness had answered a question, he's being asked the same thing over and over again. We have the same answer given to the previous question and to the most recent one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Djurdjic. Carry on, please, Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Did you -- well, you said that you followed what was happening in the news. Did you follow both the international and the local news media?

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, the statement that I was following the media, I would like to say that I received the Serbian dailies in my office and I perused them. Of course I followed the TV news. I don't speak English, and I didn't follow any international media, television, radio, or whatever. Due to my lack of foreign knowledge -- lack of knowledge of foreign languages, I couldn't follow that. I was just following the media in Serbia.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: Could the counsel please switch off the microphone while the witness is speaking. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Could we have a look at 06008.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: This is a news report in the -- or dated the 5th of April, 1999, that we took from the archives of the "New York Times" newspaper. Look at the second paragraph of that news report.

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: It reports about Suva Reka. It says: "... the richest man in town, who had rented his houses to international monitors of the Organisation for Security and Co-operation in Europe, was executed by the Serbian police at his front door along with most of his family ..." If you look at page 2 in English, page 3 in the B/C/S. At the bottom of page 2 in English, top of page 3 in B/C/S, a witness is quoted here as saying that: "She had heard from a family friend late the next day that Mr. Berisha, his three brothers, and most of their families had been executed a few yards from their house. "Mr. Berisha's cousin ... said he watched from his window as the Serbian policemen shoot Mr. Berisha, his three brothers, and two other cousins a few feet from Mr. Berisha's house, sometime between noon and 1.00 p.m. on March 26. He believed that the others, men, women, and children, were taken around to the back and shot ..." This is the Suva Reka incident. Now, Mr. Djordjevic, now listen again, I make the distinction between an allegation and knowledge that the crime was committed, and I represent to you -- I put to you, that the world knew of these allegations of these gross crimes being committed against these people by Serbian security forces. The world knew. Right across the Atlantic to the tiny islands of the Caribbean, the world knew of these allegations. Are you telling the Court that as chief of public -- chief of the police in Serbia you sat in Belgrade and did not hear even a rumour about these allegations?

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am telling you here and now, this is the first time that I have seen this article from "New York Times." As for the incident in Suva Reka, I first learned about it when criminal proceedings were instituted in Serbia, that is to say, I learned about it from newspapers. This is all I know about Suva Reka. So please understand, there were events, there were crimes committed, but I didn't know about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Nobody briefed you that this is what people were hearing all over the world, that the Serbian police was committing massacres against Kosovo Albanian civilians, including women and children? Nobody briefed you about that at all?

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Please, how do you call these wars in the press? I don't remember the exact term. But there were various things, there were various articles being written. Some crimes were never mentioned, some crimes were mentioned. But I don't know what was true and what was not true. Therefore, what the international propaganda did or whether it was propaganda at all, I don't know. I never read about this. I told you when I first heard about the Suva Reka incident. And now when I hear witnesses here giving testimony, I realise that some things had been done that are totally in contravention with the understanding. But at that moment, I was not aware of that. I only heard about that once the proceedings were instituted.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: If we could move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Your Honours, could this document be given an exhibit number?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Djurdjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I object to this document being admitted into evidence. I don't see any foundation for that whatsoever.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: The document will be received, Mr. Stamp, because of its potential relevance to the state of international knowledge and international controversy.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It, on the evidence, does not come directly close to the accused, as we see things at the moment.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that will be Exhibit P1514.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Could we look at 06009.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: This is another news report taken from the archives of the "New York Times" of Wednesday, the 7th of April, 1999. And if we look at page 2 in English, which is the top of page 3 in B/C/S. The article reports and puts in the public domain many allegations of crimes committed by Serbian forces in Kosovo. And the purpose of my asking these questions is to ask -- is inquire about your knowledge of what was happening in the public domain. It says: "A second refugee today confirmed an account of Serbian forces using a back hoe to dig a mass grave at Mala Krusa, one of two adjacent villages, where a half-dozen witnesses have described mass killings of roughly a hundred people." And it goes on to describe other alleged offences against civilians. This is what was in the public domain. The world, as I said, knew about this. Didn't you know that the world knew about the Mala Krusa massacre? Weren't you told about these allegations?

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You may or may not believe me. I heard about Mala Krusa here at this Tribunal. That was the first and the only time that I heard about this. I never heard any word about it; I never read anything about it. I heard about it here once I had an opportunity to review the indictment, and that is when I heard about all these crimes that are contained in the indictment.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Your Honours, I tender this one on the same basis and ask that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that will be Exhibit P1515.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Did you -- among the publications that you read, did you read publication "Vreme"?

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I never read that newspaper.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: If we could have a look at 06007.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I'm putting to you, Mr. Djordjevic, that in the Serbian press as well in 1999 there were allegations of serious crimes being committed against Kosovo Albanian civilians. This is the "Vreme" issue number 445 of the 17th of July, 1999. If you look to page 1, third or fourth paragraph down, it says in regard to expulsions: "In the three months of war, almost 700.000 of the Albanian residents were deported from Kosovo. Many of their houses were burnt and looted. The investigation by international experts who are working on several mass graves in Kosovo at the moment should show how many of them were killed and in what way." If we go to page 2 in the English, and this is the middle of page 1 in the B/C/S. Second paragraph of page 2: "There is no ... doubt now: The state military, police, and paramilitary forces committed horrible crimes in Kosovo." Paragraph 4: "A teacher from Kosovo (mobilised into the special units during the war) who came to the Ministry of Education to collect his salary, said how they used to fight Albanians, how they were setting their houses on fire, expelling them to the sound of the 'gusle.' When asked why they did this and what is he going to do now, he shrugged his shoulders: 'First of all: It was a directive and secondly we thought they would never return' ... "a partial sobering" -- well, there is a reference here to the reaction of the "Serbian Orthodox church, more precisely of patriarch Pavle who, during his stay in Kosovo in June," which would be June of 1999, "was stunned by the extent of the crime in Pec." And also the reaction of the Bishop of Raska and Prizren Artemije? This was in the public domain in Serbia, these allegations 1999. Are you saying to this Court, Mr. Djordjevic, that you never heard about these allegations at that time?

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I said here, in most general terms, without any specific knowledge, as was the case in all war-torn zones, in line with this most general knowledge, it could be that crimes had happened. But please understand that my primary responsibility and my focus was on Serbia outside of the territory of Kosovo. So if any person got killed, either on this side or the other side, my attention was exclusively and primarily focused on this area outside of Kosovo and Metohija. I really didn't have any knowledge. I didn't read this. I didn't have any concrete knowledge about any crime. I told you that about the heinous crimes and the localities where they took place is something that I learned about at this Court.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: As chief of the police for Serbia in 1999, didn't you receive intelligence briefings every day as to what was happening in all of Serbia?

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that's a very broad question. We all know here what I was being informed about and in what way, both from Kosovo and from the rest of the territory of Serbia, for which I was responsible. I deliberately didn't want to talk about this here in order to avoid any comparison of the crimes that I personally witnessed in Serbia, starting with the bombing of the television -- the hospitals, the sanatoriums, et cetera. I don't want to talk about it. There were terrible victims on both sides. What I mentioned right now was something that I personally witnessed, and I was personally responsible for that territory. And I never received a single piece of official information from any structures about what had happened in Kosovo.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Before I move on --

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Your Honours, could this report in the "Vreme" magazine also be received in evidence on the same basis?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Djurdjic, you repeat your objection?

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that will be Exhibit P1516.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Could we move quickly to 65 ter number 05225. I'll get the exhibit number shortly, and it's P1474. Your Honour, I wonder if it's a convenient time because I might be going into this document extensively.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. I think I will not proceed to use this document and go straight to 6010, which is P1508. And can we go straight to page 6 -- or page 5 in English, which is the top of page 7 in B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: This is part of your testimony on the 29th of June this year.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: 26th of June?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: 26th of June, I'm so sorry, 26th of June this year.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And you were asked by the Presiding Judge about some information which he characterised as relatively insignificant that came to your attention in respect to an offence. To quote the judge, he said: "I would like to know how you came to know that somewhere down there in Prokuplje or other some people had crossed the state border illegally, were tried and sentenced, and so on. Do you understand? To me, this looks like a relatively insignificant -- practically insignificant offence to be reported to someone with a very high position in the police." And your response was: "It was also for me a very routine kind of information, but as it referred to foreign citizens, it was not actually just a small deal, especially given that they were members of the Kosovo Liberation Army and that this happened immediately after our return" --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Would you mind reading slowly. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: "-- from Kosovo. So this was a rather routine information for me, but the incident itself was not really so insignificant. Everything that was happening in the organs of the interior was for the most part brought to my attention through regular channels or in some other way." That is what the -- that is what you told the Court then. The question is: Apart from the regular channels, what other ways were information about what was happening in the organs of the interior brought to your attention?

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: For example, an official -- an officer could come to me directly and tell me whatever he had to say. So there were no other special methods for me to acquire information. When they say "regular channels," they meant by telephone or somebody coming personally and conveying whatever it is they had to convey.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Incidentally, that's you speaking, not somebody else. You meant that somebody would come to you personally and convey to you information?

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If there was need for that, if they had to tell me something about some regular, routine activities and tasks or if such an officer had a proposal he would come, give it to me, ask for my opinion, that sort of thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Apart from the -- withdrawn. Could I ask you this: You were receiving in the regular reporting from the MUP staff information as to the approximate numbers of Kosovo Albanians who were crossing the border into Macedonia -- into Albania and Macedonia, weren't you?

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It wasn't me receiving. It was everybody to whom the information was addressed, the minister, various assistant ministers, and I was among the list of addressees.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Let's just take as -- for example two of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: If we could look at P701.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: This is the daily report from Mr. Lukic of the 25th of April, 1999. We have discussed -- I think you discussed some others of these when you gave evidence in chief. There is just one part I would like to go straight to. That's page 5 of the English, the last page, I think, of the B/C/S. And if you look at item 4, it gives the breakdown of Kosovo Albanian citizens leaving on the 24th of April, 1999. And in the last paragraph of that section it says: "Between the 24th of March and the 24th of April, 1999, a total of 669.071 Siptars left the FRY ..." You were receiving that type of information on a daily basis, were you?

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I would receive just like other users. Let me explain the technical procedure to you. So this paper that you're just putting to me would be sent to the chef de cabinet --

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- yes, I would receive this information, but let me explain you how. So chef de cabinet would receive this information, this report. He would go over it, and then come to me and tell me, "This is the important bit, that is the important bit." I didn't read, myself, personally all of it. There was other information there as well about what duty services reported. So I didn't read it in the sense that I knew of every sentence, no. When chef de cabinet thought that I should be informed of something, he would tell me about this; if he didn't tell me about it, then I didn't know about it. As for this particular piece of information, I did know it.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And if we could look at another one just to make a correction. This is P694, the same type of daily reporting from Mr. Lukic dated the 1st of May, 1999. If we go straight to page 8 in the English, which is the last page in the B/C/S. Again, we are looking at item 4. Similarly, the breakdown is given for those Kosovo Albanians who left the territory on the 30th of April. Now, if we look in the last paragraph you see: "Between the 24th of April and the 30th of April ... a total of 715.158 persons belonging to the Siptar national minority left the territory of the SRJ ..." Just to correct something. This would be an error, wouldn't it, if -- it should be the 24th of March, between the 24th of March and the 30th of April, 1999?

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wouldn't be able to correct it, but it is possible that it pertains to the period from the beginning of the war, which was the 24th of March. It doesn't say here how many Serbs and other non-Albanians left the territory of Kosovo and Metohija, and there were a lot of such people who left due to the war activities. And it also doesn't say here what were the reasons for these people to leave the territory. This report just gives numbers.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Okay --

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: But it doesn't explain what prompted them to leave the territory.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: As a lawyer and a police chief, Mr. Djordjevic, did you know of the organisation called Human Rights Watch during 1999?

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have heard of that organisation.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I was asking you about 1999. You -- did you become aware of a report they issued and circulated, and it was widely circulated, in October 1998 regarding the events at the Jashari compound and in Cirez and Likosane at the same time? And I'm referring to Exhibit 741, that's the 1st of October, 1998, Human Rights Watch report.

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I'm not aware of what they wrote about the event. I do know about the event, though. Now, as to how they reported on it, I don't know. I didn't read it, and I wasn't aware of their article.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: In the report they speak of the operations and they say that 83 people were killed, including 24 women and children. And at page 32 to 33 of the report -- actually, pages 30 to 33 of the report they give specific examples of incidents where excessive force or unlawful force was used by Serbian security forces, in particular the police, resulting in the deaths of many of these people. Were you aware at least that Human Rights Watch was criticising the Serbian police in the way they conducted themselves during these operations?

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really didn't know of any evaluations or assessments of theirs in relation to the operation that had been carried out. Now, as to how qualified they were to do that and what they had at that disposal to come up with that evaluation, I don't know. I don't know how they made that evaluation and what their final conclusion was.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I think Mr. Fred Abrahams testified about how they did it, and the methodology is clearly described in the Human Rights Watch report. But you were shown, when you testified in chief, a document, which is D424, which is a press release from the MUP dated 5th of March, 1998, which you said was for the purpose of denying lies in domestic and foreign media. And I assumed from that that you were aware of these reports in the domestic and foreign media about police excessive force, but you didn't agree with them.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: If you could bring up that document, D424, which is the MUP press release.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Just to remind you about that document and perhaps you could remember your earlier testimony. Don't you recall, Mr. Djordjevic, that the local and foreign press at that time were making allegations that the security forces, including the police, acted excessively, resulting in loss of life of many Albanian civilians?

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could I see the second page of this report, please. Yes, there is another information here, and that is one of the Republic of Serbia. It's a communique where the government speaks of the attitude of the foreign media concerning this event. In this portion here, it is not indicated that any excessive force was used. This communique or report issued by the minister's cabinet.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Mr. Djordjevic, please, this report according to you is a report which denies lies in the domestic and foreign media. My question is: Having a look at this denial of the allegations in the domestic and the foreign media, do you now recall --

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could I see the first page, just the first page, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Do you now recall that the local and foreign media were making allegations about the excessive force employed by the Serbian security forces, including the police, during those operations at the Jashari family compound and in Likosane and Cirez in early 1998?

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It says here: "Ministry of the Interior denies the allegations and lies launched in some domestic and foreign media about alleged torture of the arrested and detained Albanians." That is the sentence here that was released by the minister's cabinet, in which they say that these were lies, falsehoods, and alleged torture of the arrested and detained Albanians. They don't mention any foreign media reports or any excessive use of force. This statement simply denies that they were arrested, detained, and tortured.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Mr. Djordjevic, I'm asking you about your testimony, and I'm asking you specifically about your state of mind.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Djurdjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, Your Honours, Mr. Stamp put a question and you saw what kind of a question it was. I'm not going to repeat it. The witness replied based on the document. He gave a specific answer. I don't mind if Mr. Stamp continues putting his questions, but we have to make it known that the witness did reply on the question put to him; and in it he pointed out to certain things. I don't need to repeat them. The question was completely inappropriately formulated in relation to the document based on which it was put.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Your Honours, I can rephrase the question because I'm just thinking about time, though I believe --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Rephrase and move on --

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: -- because of time, Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Indeed. Thank you very much, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Mr. Djordjevic, at that time, were you not aware that the media, local media or overseas media, were making allegations that the Serbian security forces employed excessive force in the operations at the Jashari compound and in Likosane and Cirez?

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's possible that some foreign media wrote about their perception of what had happened and how it had happened. I can testify about what I know. I don't know what foreign media wrote specifically. And given the policies that were in place at the time, it is possible that the topics were different and that they wrote differently about all of the activities of the Serbian police. Now, for me to evaluate all of that, I couldn't do that. I didn't read everything. I don't know what they wrote. And they probably wrote what suited them at the time, using the events. Now, as to how objective and realistic they were at the time, I really wouldn't be able to say.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: During the summer offensive of 1999, you were aware at least that members of the MUP were involved in torching, setting on fire, houses and buildings belonging to Kosovo Albanian civilians, were you? 1998. During the operations in 1998, the anti-terrorist operations in 1998, you were aware that the Serbian security forces, in particular the police, some of them were engaged in torching buildings and property of Kosovo Albanians, were you not?

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Now this conclusion about Serbian security forces, and in particular the police, is arbitrary. I can tell you how this came about. It is true that there were instances of torching, but not in the way that you describe it now. As I have said earlier, in breaking down barricades, in neutralising terrorists, in breaking down resistance, and in anti-terrorist activities, yes, there were some facilities there were damaged and burned. And those were the main reasons and the main cases where facilities were damaged and torched. Beyond that, in individual cases, there were also instances of damage and burning and perhaps even looting of some individual houses. But I do not know who the people who did it were. When I was out in the field, yes, I did see that there had been such cases, and I did inform the gatherings, the people that I met, about what I had seen. And I insisted that whenever it was established that people had burned and damaged facilities and in case -- wherever I learned that they had done things that are unlawful, I insisted on something -- that something be done against them.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Didn't you know that policemen -- I'm not asking you about any specific individual, but policemen were involved in torching Kosovo Albanian houses and in looting Kosovo Albanian property?

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I knew that there were such cases. Wherever it was established that this was done by a policeman, measures were taken against him for looting, robbery, and burning. I cannot say exactly how many cases there were of this nature, but I know that from staff level it was insisted that members of the police act in accordance with the law and professionally, that is to say, all these activities that you referred to just now were prohibited, looting, burning, arson, et cetera. There were quite a few cases when people were dismissed from the service and when disciplinary and criminal proceedings were instituted against them. So that was the position of the leadership, and the commanders who were on the ground were also of the same view, that such negative conduct was to be prevented. Unfortunately, it wasn't done each and every time.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: In 1998, were you aware of the United Nations Security Council Resolution 1160 of the 31st of March, 1998, that "condemned" - and I will quote - "the use of excessive force by the Serbian police force against civilians"?

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I did not study it in detail, but I know that there was this Resolution 1160, and I think there was 1166, where such activities are indicated. And also there is the request for the Albanian leadership to dissociate itself from terrorist activities in Kosovo and Metohija at the time, that is to say that the Security Council knew then that this had to do with terrorist activities, and they wanted the leadership of the Albanians to dissociate themselves from that kind of thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I think you mentioned another resolution. There's another one I want to ask you about. 1199, UN Security Council Resolution 1199 of the 23rd of September, 1998, which expressed grave concern, in particular the excessive and indiscriminate use of force by the Yugoslav security forces and the VJ which have resulted in numerous civilian casualties. Do you recall that one?

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember, I don't know the exact name of the resolution, but I know that this resolution preceded all the political discussions that took place afterwards aimed at preventing the escalation of further activity in the territory of Kosovo by the Serb forces and also that the terrorist forces there refrain from their terrorist activities. As far as I can remember at this point in time, and in I'm not mistaken, that is what it was all about. And, of course, this resolution also says what you had referred to.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Just for the record, Your Honours, may I just indicate that the first resolution I referred to is P1074 and the second one is D160.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Did you, Mr. Djordjevic - and I'm moving on now - at any time set up a commission or a body specifically charged with responsibility to investigate allegations of crimes committed by the police in Kosovo during 1999?

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I did not establish any commission or body.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: You told us in your testimony that you did what the minister ordered you to do because you thought he was threatening you. Did you, Mr. Djordjevic, mention this alleged threat in any of your previous accounts before coming to Court to testify over the last two weeks, in any of your previous accounts about the reasons why you participated in the concealment of the bodies?

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I always said that I worked on the minister's orders and that I carried out his orders. As for the conversations I had with him, it is unequivocal that, in order to have these tasks carried out, he assumes that my life is threatened. That is what I wanted to say, and that is the truth.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Did you -- well, I represent to you - I don't want us to have to go through these documents - I represent to you that in your letter in 2004 where you referred to obeying these instructions from the minister to conceal the bodies and in your opening statement where you also referred to this -- to these events, you did not say that you acted partly or entirely as a result of a threat or your belief that there was a threat. This was something that you said recently, over the last two weeks when you came to testify here.

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because of my activities or non-compliance with the minister's orders, I spoke about that in that letter and later. My life was being threatened specifically by the minister and by others. Now, whether I said everything in minute detail in that particular letter, well I know how I did this, why I did this, and why I had to do it.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Mr. Djordjevic, are you saying that in your letter of 2004 you said that you obeyed the minister's orders in respect to concealment of the bodies because he threatened you? That is not in the letter, Mr. Djordjevic, so I want to know if you are telling the Court that you said that in that letter.

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Please, in that letter I addressed the public. I could not say everything in detail. I wrote that letter in revolt and some kind of rage. There were a few elementary mistakes in all of that, in this letter. It wasn't for me now to deal with each and every detail that I knew. I could have written a letter on 200 pages then, and I don't know how many pages this testimony is. My life was endangered then; it was endangered after the 5th of October too. Now, whether I put all of that in the right places in your view, that's a different matter. I know under which conditions I worked. At the moment when I was supposed to be ordered to use a weapon to kill someone, I energetically refused to do that. As for bodies of persons who had already been killed, I could no longer help these persons --

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Mr. Djordjevic --

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- I did take action then knowing that I was not guilty at all in respect to the death of these persons.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Yes, we have heard that. I am focusing now - and I would ask you, please, to focus on that - on this -- the evidence of yours that you were threatened by the minister. You recall, Mr. Djordjevic, that you were also asked quite extensive questions about your motivations for obeying [Realtime transcript read in error "being"] the minister by your attorney when you testified in chief for over a week. And again, Mr. Djordjevic, I represent to you that you did not mention this threat during your testimony in chief. And I ask you: Why did you fail to refer to it when your attorney asked you about it or asked you about the circumstances of that event?

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't understand now. What is it that I did say and what is it that I did not say during my examination-in-chief? Could you be more specific. I think that I did say during my examination-in-chief that I did this because -- because I was ordered to do so and because I was told to take care of myself in that sense. When he told me to take care of myself, it was my understanding that I was supposed to safe-guard my life. Now, that is my assumption. Now, how you understood this, this is something -- well, I cannot repeat each and every word that I said. I understood this as a most serious threat in relation to my very own life.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Djurdjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Again, we are dealing with the problem of the way in which Mr. Stamp puts his questions, and then he gives his comment with regard to some answer, and he's not giving a specific reference as to what it was that had actually happened. After this evidence, I am going to give the Court all the references that Mr. Stamp invoked and what is actually stated there. But could he say specifically what he said during the examination-in-chief. Let us not hear Mr. Stamp's conclusions. Since this is being put to the witness, why doesn't he put to the witness his very own words, not put the questions the way he is putting them, Mr. Stamp that is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Carry on, please, Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: All I'm saying to you, Mr. Djordjevic, is that you failed to say that you were threatened in your entire examination-in-chief. Is there a reason why you failed to explain to the Court that you felt threatened and that is why you did what you did?

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what to answer to you now. If I was ordered and told to take care of myself, Take care of yourself and take care and respect of what you're doing, that was the most serious threat that I received. And I took it as a most serious threat in relation to my own life. Now, how you interpret it is something -- well --

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Very well --

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- I took those words in that sense.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Very well. Let's move to the 9th of July, 1999 -- or is it the 9th of -- were you at a meeting --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Djurdjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Transcript page 42; 24, 25, those were the lines. I think it says "minister." It says your motivation to be minister. That is what the transcript says.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I think it's "to obey," not "to be." "To obey the minister." That's how it should read.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Carry on, please, Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Do you recall a meeting after the war in 1999 attended by representatives, senior representatives, of the MUP including yourself and the minister and also of the VJ in which the events in the war was reviewed or were reviewed? And Mr. Stojiljkovic gave a report as to -- that included crimes committed by members of the MUP. Do you recall that meeting?

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that is your totally free interpretation of what had happened at that meeting. I attended the meeting, and the minister did not submit a report about what had happened during the course of the war --

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Very well --

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- that was --

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: What was the date of this meeting?

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't know what the date was, but it was sometime around the 10th of July. How could I know now ? It was after the war, this meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: According to Mr. Vasiljevic in his testimony - and that's at transcript 5725 to 6 - he said that Mr. Stojiljkovic said that only -- that there were only 13 MUP members who committed crimes, and procedures had been initiated accordingly in each case. Do you recall the minister saying that?

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I recall that he did talk about that. As for the number of persons or the number of crimes committed -- well, I remember that he mentioned the casualties, the killed and the wounded, and the general situation, the co-operation between the army and the police. And, of course, he talked about the crimes that were known of at the time and what kind of steps were taken against the members of the police who had done that, as had been established. So that was one of the topics. There were other topics too --

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Very well --

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- meaning.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: -- I just wanted to get your comment on what he said about the MUP crimes, which is that he did talk about that. We could move on to something else very quickly, and that is the Skorpions.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I think we need to go into closed session for this, Your Honours. I have to refer to the testimony of K92.
